corrected_draft.title: SEC Filing Reports Ramaswamy Held 8.4% of Strive
corrected_draft.description_short: An SEC amendment reported Vivek Ramaswamy beneficially owned 5,693,897 Strive shares, or 8.4%, in a filing tied to an April 20, 2026 event.
corrected_draft.description_medium: An SEC Schedule 13D amendment reported that Vivek Ramaswamy beneficially owned 5,693,897 shares of Strive, Inc., equal to 8.4% of the class on the filing’s stated conversion assumption. The filing identifies April 20, 2026 as the event date. It says the issuer’s at-the-market share sales ended the shareholder agreement and dissolved the reporting group; Ramaswamy continued to own more than 5%. The amendment does not support the held record’s 7.6% figure or May 28 date.
corrected_draft.description_long: An SEC Schedule 13D amendment filed by Vivek Ramaswamy and other reporting persons states that he beneficially owned 5,693,897 Strive, Inc. shares, representing 8.4% of the class under the filing’s stated assumption that Class B shares convert to Class A. The filing identifies April 20, 2026 as the event date. It explains that Strive’s at-the-market share sales increased the number of outstanding shares, causing the reporting group to fall below the 50% voting-power threshold in its shareholder agreement. The agreement then terminated automatically, and the reporting persons ceased to constitute a group. The amendment says Ramaswamy still beneficially owned more than 5% and would report separately; the other exiting persons fell below 5%. This establishes an ownership disclosure and reporting change. It does not support the held entry’s claim of a 7.6% stake as of May 28, nor any assertion that his Ohio policy platform was designed to benefit Strive investors.

corrected_draft.description_long: On June 16, 2026, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington reported that Donald Trump had visited resorts and golf courses he still profits from on 191 of the first 512 days of his second term, equal to 37% of those days. CREW also counted 259 individual property visits, including 148 visits to golf courses; that number exceeds the day count because more than one property visit can occur in a single day. The article lists 102 visits to Mar-a-Lago and says Secret Service records showed nearly $100,000 spent at Trump properties in the first few months of the second term. It notes that the amount excludes costs from other agencies and discusses Air Force One operating costs by citing a Palm Beach Post analysis. The article does not establish the held entry’s $115 million cumulative travel-and-security figure or its $300 million end-of-term projection. Those totals need a separate auditable source and methodology.

corrected_draft.description_long: On March 27, 2025, the Social Security Administration issued a release correcting reports that it was permanently closing local field offices. SSA said it had not permanently closed or announced the permanent closure of any local field office since January 1 of that year. The agency separately acknowledged that it had announced one permanent hearing-office closure, in White Plains, New York. SSA said it works with congressional delegations before permanent closures and reassigns employees from affected offices to other locations. It also explained that many spaces identified to the General Services Administration for possible lease termination were small hearing rooms with no assigned employees, as most hearings were held virtually. The agency said temporary local-office closures can occur because of weather, damage, or facilities problems, followed by reopening. These statements do not support the entry’s claim that DOGE had already closed at least ten field offices or that the White Plains decision was a new DOGE closure.

corrected_draft.title: 2025 Law Retains CHIP Enrollment Protections While Narrowing Some Immigrant Eligibility
corrected_draft.description_short: The 2025 law retained several CHIP protections but separately narrowed Medicaid and CHIP eligibility for many lawful immigrants.
corrected_draft.description_medium: Georgetown’s post-enactment analysis says the July 4, 2025 reconciliation law retained separate-state CHIP protections against waiting periods, missed-premium lockouts, annual or lifetime limits, and coverage gaps during transitions. The law separately limits Medicaid and CHIP eligibility for many lawfully present immigrants beginning October 1, 2026. The original claim that states could restore the listed CHIP restrictions is incorrect.
corrected_draft.description_long: President Donald Trump signed the 2025 reconciliation law, P.L. 119-21, on July 4, 2025. Georgetown’s Center for Children and Families reviewed the enacted provisions and reports that several key protections for children in separate state CHIP programs remained in effect: states could not impose CHIP waiting periods, lock out children over missed premiums, or apply annual or lifetime dollar limits, and Medicaid and CHIP agencies still had to coordinate eligibility transitions. The same law contains separate changes to immigrant eligibility. The analysis says section 71109 removes Medicaid and CHIP eligibility for many lawfully present immigrants, including refugees and asylees, effective October 1, 2026, while retaining eligibility for specified groups such as green-card holders after five years and certain other categories. The held claim that the law restored waiting periods and lockouts is wrong. These distinct provisions should not be collapsed into a claim that all children’s coverage protections were removed.
